full_judgment:
2. The short fact leading to these petitions is that, Ibrahim Shah Waqf Estate was earlier enrolled under EC No. 3543 by an order dated 7-7-1981. Administrator of Waqf in exercise of power under section 51 of the Waqf Ordinance appointed the appellant and three others namely, Abdul Wahab Shah Chowdhury, Abdus Satter Shah Chowdhury and Hajee Hasan Shah Chowdhury who are respondents in both the appeals joint Mutwallis of the Waqf Estate. Against this order Abdul Wahab Shah Chowdhury and Abdul Quayyum Shah Chowdhury, beneficiaries, preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 129 of 1981 before the learned District Judge, Rajshahi under section 43 of the aforesaid Ordinance. Abdus Satter Shah Chowdhury also preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 153 of 1981 before the said Court. After creation of district at Naogaon the said two appeals were transferred to the Court of District Judge, Noagaon and renumbered as Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 18-19 of 1984. These appeals were fixed for hearing on 17-1-1996. But due to non-appearance from the side of the appellants those were dismissed for default by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Naogaon. Then Miscellaneous Case Nos. 3-4 of 1996 under Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure were filed for restoration of these two appeals on the same ground. They alleged that after transfer of the appeals from Rajshahi to Naogaon they have been prosecuting the appeals by engaging lawyers but their lawyers did not take necessary steps which led to the dismissal of the appeals and they came to know of the same in November 1996 for the first time. They then along with the appellants filed a petition under Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They also filed applications for condonation of delay in filing the petitions. The matter was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Naogaon who condoned the delay and allowed the Miscellaneous Case restoring the appeals to their original files and numbers for ends of justice by orders dated 24-8-1997. The petitioners then filed Civil Revision Nos. 3730 and 3731 of 1997 before the High Court Division but a Single Judge of that Division discharged the Rules refusing to interfere with the matter. 

 3. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division misdirected itself in law in taking the view that both section 5 of the Limitation Act and Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be applied to appeals filed under section 43 of the Waqf Ordinance and whether the High Court Division has committed wrong in upholding the orders of restoration of the appeals made by the learned Additional District Judge upon a wrong assumption that the appellants have no knowledge of the transfer of the appeals in question from Rajshahi to Naogaon and whether the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division have committed error of law in condoning the delay in preferring Miscellaneous Case and restoring the appeals for ends of justice. 

 5. Mr ABM Nurul Islam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that filing of appeals under section 43 of the Waqf Ordinance on being aggrieved by an order of the Administrator is a substantive right and if an appeal is dismissed for default, an application under Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure for readmission of the appeal can be maintained as it is a procedural matter. He submits that the word ''decision'' of the District Judge means final adjudication pronouncing judgment on the merit of the appeal which does not include the order of dismissal of the appeal on default. He submits that the dispute is of civil nature and the District Judge acts not as a persona designate but as a Court in deciding appeals filed under the Waqf Ordinance. Therefore for readmission or disposal of the appeal, the Court has to follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure as there is no other procedure prescribed by any other law for this purpose. It is submitted that the Court cannot be armless, it has to proceed with the appeal for final adjudication. He further submits that there is no scope for thinking that the District Judge as referred to in section 43 of the Waqf Ordinance is a persona designata. It is a Court. In deciding appeals filed under section 43 of the Ordinance, he is to follow the Code of Civil Procedure. He submits that the civil Court is entitled to try all kinds of suits of civil nature unless the same is specifically barred under any specific provision of the law and in the present case there is no such bar. Learned Advocate further submits that from the materials on record it would appear that the appeals were dismissed for default, due to no fault of respondents but due to laches on the part of their Advocates. The respondents were not informed by the learned Advocate about the date of hearing of the appeal and in such a situation the learned Additional District Judge has not committed any wrong or illegality in readmitting the appeals under Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 6. The first point raised in these appeals is on the applicability of Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the present cases. 

 7. Mr MA Wahhab Miah submits that when the decision of the learned Additional District Judge is final, the remedy available to the respondents is in the form of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr Wahhab Miah further submits that the effect of dismissal of the appeals for default is an ex parte dismissal of the appeals. And in such a situation provisions of Order 41 rule 19 of the Code are not applicable. In support of his submissions Mr Wahhab Miah placed reliance in the case of Abdul Kader Chowdhury vs Nurul Islam and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 128 where it has been held that the effect of an order of dismissal of Miscellaneous Cage in default in rejecting an application to set aside a decree passed ex parte, is not an order passed on merit but ex parte. From this decision Mr Wahhab Mia tried to impress that the order of dismissal of the appeals in the present case is a final order. 

 8. Here in the present case the main question is, whether the provisions of Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure is available to the appellants when their appeals were dismissed for default. It is nobody's case that the "District Judge" as mentioned in section 43 of the Waqf Ordinance is a persona designate. Mr Wahhab Miah frankly conceded that the District Judge here is not a persona designate but a Court. Section 43 of Ordinance provided that an appeal against the order of appointment of Mutawalli shall have to be filed before the District Judge. Excepting this nothing has been mentioned in this section or in the Ordinance how the District Judge is to deal with the appeals. When this is the position the District Judge shall follow the procedures as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure in disposing of the appeals filed before him. In deciding the point raised we may very well consider the provision of section 108 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This section provides for an application of the provisions regarding appeals from orders made under the Code or under other special law for which there is no other procedure for appeal. In the Waqf Ordinance no procedure has been mentioned how the District Judge is to dispose of the appeals. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure relates to procedural matters and it provides that the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits shall be followed as far as it can be made applicable in all proceeding in any Court of civil jurisdiction and section 121 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that the Rules in the First Schedule shall have effect as if enacted in the body of this Code unless and until annulled or altered in accordance with the provisions of Part X of the Code. From a consideration of the provisions of the Code as well as section 43 of the Waqf Ordinance it appears that as the District Judge as contemplated under section 43 of the Waqf Ordinance is not a persona designata but a Court and as it is a Court of civil nature, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure is very much attracted in the present case and accordingly, the provisions of Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure is available to the respondents. Mr Wahhab Miah earlier placed reliance in the case of Abdul Kader Chowdhury vs Nurul Islam and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 128 and tried to impress that as the appeals were dismissed for default the respondents had remedy available in revisional applications but this decision has no application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 11. Since the provisions of Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure are available to the appellants before the appellate Court, this submission has also no force. We also find from the impugned judgments and the judgments of the Court below that the respondents made out an acceptable case that they were prevented from appearing when the appeals were called on for hearing for sufficient reasons. The appellate Court as well as the High Court Division has not committed any wrong in restoring the appeals to their original files and numbers. There is therefore no merit in these appeals.
